claims.text: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr can be synthesized using powder-based processing followed by sintering.
The sintered alloy contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The alloy has a defect-rich, chemically disordered BCC microstructure.
The proposed framework calculates electronic and lattice thermal-conductivity components separately.
The electronic calculation omits defect scattering.
The lattice calculation explicitly includes anharmonic phonon-phonon interactions, compositional disorder, and oxygen-interstitial scattering.
Oxygen interstitials and associated defects modify phonon mean free paths in HfNbTaTiZr.
Summing separately calculated lattice and electronic contributions avoids conflating the two transport channels.
Earlier models for this alloy assumed perfect, defect-free bulk crystals and conflated lattice and electronic transport.
Earlier analytical models produced errors of 30–50% or more relative to experiment.
The new model will outperform earlier approaches and predict total thermal conductivity within ±10% over 300–1200 K.
Measured total thermal conductivity for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen is 10–17 W/(K·m) over 300–1200 K.
Below approximately 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions are comparable.
At higher temperatures, transport becomes lattice dominated because oxygen defects increase phonon scattering.
Prediction uncertainty increases below approximately 200 K because decoupling the lattice and electronic contributions becomes less distinct.
The claimed accuracy applies only to similarly sintered or powder-metallurgy HfNbTaTiZr samples with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and comparable microstructures.
Failure to match total conductivity within ±10% over 300–1200 K, or substantial disagreement in separately measured lattice and electronic components, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes a high-temperature lattice-dominated regime to increased phonon scattering from oxygen defects. Increased phonon scattering ordinarily suppresses the lattice contribution; no stronger reduction of the electronic contribution is stated that would make lattice transport dominant.
